title: How to Measure Account-Level NPS Across Multiple Stakeholders in B2B
summary: Tag responses by account and role, report NPS by role, roll up with a deliberate method, flag silent decision-makers, and tie results to renewal.
body_markdown:
One B2B account can send back five net promoter score (NPS) responses that disagree with each other. The executive sponsor gives you a 9. The admin who fights your permissions model every week gives you a 4. The VP who signs the renewal never answers. Average those scores and you get a number that describes nobody.


To measure account-level NPS across multiple stakeholders, tag every response with its account and the respondent's role. Report NPS by role first. Then roll individual scores up to an account view using a method you choose on purpose: a simple average, a role-weighted score, or a decision-maker rule. Track role coverage next to the score, so a silent economic buyer shows up as a gap. Then read the open-ended comments by role, and tie the account view to renewal dates and contract value. Thematic handles the comment side: it segments feedback themes by metadata such as persona and account type, and its Revenue at Risk score estimates the revenue sitting behind each theme.


Bain's Rob Markey named the core problem:[what matters most in a B2B context "isn't the aggregate score for a customer organization, which depends heavily on who is responding."](https://www.bain.com/insights/get-real-feedback-from-your-b2b-customers)


## The six-step process


1. Map the stakeholders in each account and tag every response with account and role.
2. Report NPS by role before you roll anything up.
3. Roll individual scores up to an account view, using a method you pick deliberately.
4. Measure coverage and flag the silent decision-maker.
5. Read the open-ended comments by role.
6. Tie account-level results to renewal and revenue at risk.


## Step 1: Map the stakeholders and tag every response


For each account, list the people who influence the relationship and give each one a role. Four roles cover most[B2B accounts](https://getthematic.com/insights/b2b-customer-insights) :


- **Economic buyer or executive sponsor.** Owns the budget and the renewal decision.
- **Admin or champion.** Runs the product day to day and fields internal complaints.
- **End user.** Uses the product and judges it on how their work feels.
- **Procurement or finance.** Negotiates price and terms.


[Gartner's 2025 survey of 632 B2B buyers](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-05-07-gartner-sales-survey-finds-74-percent-of-b2b-buyer-teams-demonstrate-unhealthy-conflict-during-the-decision-process) found buying groups ranging from five to 16 people across as many as four functions. The same survey found 74% of B2B buyer teams show unhealthy conflict during the buying decision.


Then add role and account ID fields to every response. Pull them from your customer relationship management (CRM) system at send time, not from respondents. A response without both can't be rolled up or interpreted.


## Step 2: Report NPS by role before you roll up


Before you build an account score, calculate standard[NPS](https://getthematic.com/insights/ultimate-guide-to-net-promoter-score) for each role across your whole customer base. This tells you what your account scores will be made of.


Roles score differently for predictable reasons. Bain notes that "procurement people may assess your offerings primarily on price, delivery, terms," while "end users are likely to judge you more on features, ease of use and service."


Skip this step and you miss the composition problem. If end users are 60% of responses and score lower than executives, every account score is really an end-user score.


## Step 3: Roll individual scores up to an account view


There's no single correct rollup. Each method answers a different question and fails in a different way. Pick one, document it, and keep it stable so trends mean something.


**Method** **How it works** **What it answers** **Main trade-off**


Simple average Average all 0 to 10 scores in the account How does the account feel overall? Dominated by whichever role responds most, usually end users


Account NPS Promoters minus detractors, as a share of respondents in the account Is the account net positive? Unstable with three or four respondents; one answer swings it 25 points or more


Role-weighted average Weight each role (for example, 40% economic buyer, 30% admin, 20% users, 10% procurement) How does the account feel, adjusted for influence on renewal? Weights are a judgment call and can hide a loud, unhappy user base


Decision-maker rule Account takes the score of the economic buyer, with a flag if any other role is a detractor Will the person who signs renew? Throws away most of the data and fails completely when the buyer is silent


Many programs pair two of these. A role-weighted score is the headline. A decision-maker flag sits next to it, so a happy user base can't hide a detractor sponsor.


Set role weights from evidence, not instinct. Check which roles' scores have tracked renewal and expansion in your own book, and revisit the weights once a year.


## Step 4: Measure coverage and flag the silent decision-maker


The most dangerous response in account-level NPS is the one you never got. Six happy end users and a silent economic buyer can look strong right up to the non-renewal notice.


Track coverage as its own metric, next to the score:


- **Role coverage.** Which of the mapped roles responded in this cycle?
- **Decision-maker coverage.** Did the person who signs the renewal respond?
- **Respondent count.** How many people does the account score rest on?


Then mark any account missing its economic buyer as "unmeasured at the top," whatever its score says. Don't impute the buyer's score from other roles.


Close the gap through the relationship, not a reminder email. Bain recommends account managers ask key contacts to take part, and to "solicit feedback broadly within an organization and maintain clarity about the role of the people responding." If the buyer won't take a survey, ask the same question in a renewal conversation and log it.


## Step 5: Read the open-ended comments by role


The score tells you where an account stands. The comments tell you why, and the why differs by role. An executive's 6 might be about strategic fit. An admin's 6 is more likely about permissions or support.


Segment the open text by the same role field you use for the score.[Thematic's Impact Analysis](https://getthematic.com/product/business-impact-analysis) lets teams filter impact and trends by segments such as persona, region, journey stage, and account type. It shows[which themes drive NPS](https://getthematic.com/insights/link-feedback-themes-nps-csat-drivers) within each segment, so you can see that "reporting gaps" drags down executive scores while "single sign-on (SSO) setup" drags down admins. Every theme traces back to the[verbatim comments](https://getthematic.com/insights/best-tool-for-analyzing-nps-verbatims) behind it.


Two questions are worth asking of every role cut:


- **Which themes appear in one role and not the others?** These are the problems your account team is least likely to hear about.
- **Which themes cost the most points in the role that decides renewal?** Fix those first, even if another role mentions something more often.


Mitre 10, the New Zealand home improvement cooperative, reads its retail and trade feedback separately. Mark Vaughan of Mitre 10 explains why:["Our trade business feedback tends to drive more account-specific initiatives, while retail feedback requires more granular, day-to-day operational responses."](https://getthematic.com/insights/humanising-hardware-how-mitre10-made-voice-of-customer-actionable-with-thematic)


## Step 6: Tie account-level results to renewal and revenue at risk


An account score becomes a business number when you join it to commercial data. For each account, add renewal date, annual contract value, and expansion potential. Then sort. A detractor-led account renewing in 60 days with a large contract is your first call. A promoter account with no buyer coverage renewing next quarter is your second.


It matters because[B2B promoters have an average lifetime value typically three to eight times that of detractors.](https://www.netpromotersystem.com/about/building-loyalty-at-b2b-companies/)


The theme view adds the other half.[Thematic's Revenue at Risk score](https://getthematic.com/product/revenue-at-risk) estimates how much revenue sits behind each theme in your feedback. You define at-risk using score thresholds, churn themes, customer metadata, or a combination, each with a churn likelihood your team agrees on. You set customer values, such as annual contract value, for each segment. Thematic then ranks themes by revenue at risk and shows the arithmetic behind each figure.


Keep the two views distinct. Revenue at Risk is aggregate by theme, not a per-account[churn prediction](https://getthematic.com/insights/how-to-perform-churn-analysis) . The account list tells you whom to call this month. The theme ranking tells you[which fixes protect the most revenue](https://getthematic.com/insights/revenue-at-risk-customer-feedback) across every account.


Mitre 10 joins the two on its trade business. Vaughan says its B2B analysis can "link feedback to customer lifetime value and even share of wallet metrics." The same program found stock availability was costing half an NPS point.


## A worked example


Imagine a software company with an enterprise account worth $250,000 a year, renewing in four months. Five people received the relationship survey, and four responded:


- Three end users scored 8, 9, and 9.
- The admin scored 3.
- The economic buyer did not respond.


The simple average is 7.25, which looks fine. Account NPS is 25, because two of four respondents are promoters and one is a detractor. A role-weighted score can't be calculated at all, because the buyer's 40% weight is missing. The decision-maker rule returns "unmeasured."


Read together, the picture is clear. Users are happy. The admin is a detractor. The person who signs is silent. The admin's comment mentions permissions and a support ticket open for three weeks, and that theme drives most admin detractors across the customer base.


The account team books a call with the buyer and brings a fix date for the admin's issue. The customer experience (CX) team takes the permissions theme to product, ranked by the revenue behind it.


## Common mistakes to avoid


- **Averaging everyone into one number.** A single average hides the role that decides renewal. Report by role first.
- **Treating a missing buyer as neutral.** Silence from the economic buyer is a risk signal. Flag it as unmeasured.
- **Changing weights every quarter.** Shifting weights make trends meaningless. Set them from evidence and review them once a year.
- **Trusting small-sample account NPS.** Three respondents can't carry a promoter-minus-detractor score. Show the respondent count next to it.
- **Reading comments without the role field.** An admin complaint and an executive complaint need different owners. Segment the text the same way you segment the score.
- **Confusing theme revenue with account revenue.** Pricing a theme tells you what to fix. Pricing an account tells you whom to call. You need both.
